teaching_blocks.title: Errors, Slices and Subgroup Risks
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied mitigation targets a subgroup with a poor validation result. Check whether the data represents that group, then evaluate the mitigation on both the affected segment and the overall cohort. Do not assume changing the model is the only explanation or remedy.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Evaluate whether the data represents the groups for which the model is intended before attributing a subgroup problem solely to the model. Check the supplied mitigation on the affected validation segment as well as the overall validation cohort before accepting it. For a subgroup, its contribution to total expected harm is its deployment population probability multiplied by its subgroup-conditional expected harm; use the supplied error costs for that calculation.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the deployment probability of the subgroup is 0.25 and its subgroup-conditional expected harm under the supplied error costs is 0.80. Its contribution to total expected harm is 0.25 × 0.80 = 0.20. If a supplied mitigation changes the subgroup harm to 0.60, the corresponding contribution becomes 0.15 under the same population probability. Still inspect its overall validation evidence and the affected group's representation before accepting it. For any binary-rate calculation, retain the actual-negative and actual-positive denominators separately. The calculation weights conditional harm by population share; it does not turn a small evaluation sample into justified deployment representation.

The multiplication by 0.25 is the population weighting step, not a revision to the subgroup's conditional rate. Keep subgroup false-positive and false-negative conditions distinct when computing its harm. Then compare the supplied mitigation with the reference on a matched affected segment and overall cohort. An improvement in the subgroup contribution is useful evidence only under the supplied population probability and cost assumptions. Inspect representation before extending that evidence to deployment. The exercise is a bounded check of a provided mitigation; it does not authorize inventing protected categories, new policies or an untested repair that merely seems fair.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A subgroup-only improvement is not sufficient acceptance evidence. Population probability, conditional harm and representation are distinct parts of the evaluation, and empty conditioning groups do not provide error rates.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

context.concept_name: Choose a task-compatible training loss

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a task-compatible loss and verify its output, target and gradient contracts.

required_facts.statement: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#optimization_tutorial.html — Hyperparameters; Loss Function; Optimizer; Full Implementation

required_facts.statement: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C).
MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.
BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs.

For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target.
For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

segments.label: Training and forward-only validation in PyTorch
segments.summary: PyTorch provides two independent controls for validation. Calling model.train() or model.eval() changes the behavior of mode-sensitive layers such as dropout and batch normalization. A torch.no_grad() context prevents operations from recording a gradient graph; it does not replace the evaluation-mode switch. context.concept_name: Stop training using validation behavior without consulting the protected test

coverage.learning_objective: Implement a validation-patience controller that returns the best retained model state.

required_facts.statement: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement.
For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted.
Retain the model weights associated with the best monitored validation value rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model.
Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system.
Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

teaching_blocks.title: Stop and Debug Training
teaching_blocks.content:
A validation quantity improves and then stalls. Early stopping is a predeclared controller over this sequence, not a decision to use whichever epoch happened to run last. Preserve the best checkpoint accepted under the declared minimum-improvement rule while training can still alter live parameters.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement. For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted. Here, best is the validation value at the most recent checkpoint accepted under min_delta, not necessarily the lowest observed value. Retain that accepted checkpoint’s model weights rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model. Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Preserve the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights by deep copy or a saved state file, and restore that checkpoint for subsequent use rather than the last weights. Protected-test observations do not decide patience or checkpoint choice.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict reference is not necessarily a frozen best-epoch snapshot. Later updates can alter live parameter values, and ‘slightly lower’ is not sufficient improvement when it fails the declared min_delta rule.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the derivative reference predicts a negative gradient for a selected parameter, but the reproduced record shows zero. Inspect .grad after backward and before clearing it, then follow the derivative chain from loss through outputs to that parameter. Check the target representation and declared learning rate alongside the loss computation. Choose one supported root-cause hypothesis, apply its supplied correction and rerun the identical bounded fixture. Compare the corrected loss and gradient signs and magnitudes with the failing reference. A lower loss in a different task or with multiple simultaneous changes would not isolate this hypothesis. Keep assertion fixtures for both the expected computation and the reproduced failure.

The identical rerun is what makes the correction test informative. Preserve the fixture, target contract and baseline failing evidence while changing the one supported factor. If the correction is intended to restore a missing gradient path, inspect the derivative and parameter .grad at the same points as before. If the supplied cause concerns representation or learning rate, retain those resolved inputs in the comparison. Record whether the corrected bounded task meets its declared expectations, not just whether an exception disappeared. This isolates evidence for one hypothesis without claiming that all future training failures have the same cause.

teaching_blocks.content: A stalled loss does not justify arbitrary configuration changes. Gradient evidence has a timing requirement, and inspecting after zeroing gradients can hide the learning signal you intended to diagnose.

teaching_blocks.content:
For a linear layer with input width 20 and output width 10, the weight reference contains 200 elements and the bias 10. At four bytes each, those parameters alone account for 840 bytes, before gradients, activations and batch matrices are counted. Sum simultaneously live allocations using their own element widths. Inspect peak allocated and reserved evidence and whether saved diagnostics retain computation graphs. Change one supported factor, such as a smaller batch or removing an unnecessary retained graph reference, then rerun the same bounded task and verify completion and peak. Use scalar or detached diagnostic values where gradients through the saved values are not needed.

At the reproduced failure point, count only the allocations actually simultaneously live rather than adding every tensor ever created during the run. A saved graph-connected loss tensor can retain a computation reference; a scalar loss diagnostic does not need that gradient connection. Parameter element counts are another explicit component of the reference, alongside gradients, activations and batches. The allocated/reserved distinction then helps interpret the runtime observation. If the trace attributes most measured work to loading, test one supported loading factor rather than immediately changing model computation. Inspect CPU, memory and process state during the same interval; for the container fixture, docker stats and docker top provide that supporting evidence. After the change, compare the same bounded workload again without profiler overhead in the final timing. On CUDA, synchronize measurement boundaries so a CPU clock includes completed accelerator work. Keep the profiling attribution separate from the final unprofiled performance comparison, since they answer related but different questions.

The profiler trace supplies attribution, while the unprofiled rerun supplies the matched elapsed-time comparison. Keep the same bounded workload and one-factor change between those two comparisons. A loading-region label should enclose the intended loading work; a model-compute label should identify that separate work rather than blend it with setup. Runtime CPU, memory and process evidence must refer to the same window. Synchronization at accelerator timing boundaries accounts for asynchronous completion. This makes the observed difference interpretable without assuming that a profiler's overhead or a shifted measurement boundary is a genuine speed improvement.

segments.label: Guard an entry point so importing the module does not invoke it
segments.summary: Python sets a module’s __name__ to "__main__" when running its file directly and to the module’s name when importing it. Initially, a statement outside the guard executes in both cases. Moving that statement into a main function and placing its call behind if __name__ == "__main__": changes the behavior: direct execution calls main, while importing the module does not. The guard controls the entry-point call; it does not prevent other top-level statements from executing during import.

bridge_note.before: Watch how direct execution and import produce different __name__ values, then how guarding the entry-point call changes the output. The example uses ordinary Python modules, not training.
bridge_note.after: The clip establishes the entry-point guard. The text supplies the remaining training workflow: parameters, defaults and overrides, JSON loading and saving, notebook comparison, checked subprocess execution, f-string reporting, repository commits, and clean-shell output capture.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Upload the supplied dataset to the version-enabled test bucket and record its created generation and the SHA-256 digest of the local bytes. Later, select that recorded generation explicitly, verify it exists and download it. Compare the downloaded bytes' digest with the expected snapshot identity. In the authorized overwrite fixture, change only the mutable latest object, then retrieve the original generation again. The observed original digest should still match the snapshot record. Keep object name, generation and digest together: the name tells you which object family, the generation selects the version, and the digest checks the bytes you actually obtained.

The overwrite test separates immutable snapshot selection from the mutable object's current state. Verify the recorded generation exists before relying on it, and check the content after retrieval rather than assuming a version-qualified request returned the expected bytes. A local digest computed before upload and a digest of the later download can be compared directly as content evidence. Keep the selected generation in the record even when both old and latest objects happen to have the same name. The test proves retrieval of the recorded fixture, not a claim that mutable names are intrinsically safe for reproduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A mutable object name is not immutable data identity. Recording a digest without verifying downloaded bytes also does not establish that the intended snapshot was retrieved.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the local HEAD, collect pinned dependency versions with pip freeze, and record sys.version and sys.executable with the supplied runtime identity. Serialize that dictionary to the declared text manifest and parse it back. Compare the parsed revision, dependency mapping and runtime identity with independently inspected values. If the manifest says revision A but HEAD is B, reject the match rather than correcting the observed revision to fit the manifest. The dependency file can be installed with pip install -r in the declared environment. Keep the saved manifest and verified values identifiable so a later reproduction can resolve the recorded context.

The parsed manifest is the artifact a later execution will read, so inspect it after serialization rather than only inspecting the in-memory dictionary that preceded writing. Compare its dependency mapping with the freeze output, its revision with HEAD and its Python/runtime fields with the actual process. Paths such as sys.executable help identify which interpreter executed, while sys.version records that interpreter's version information. Keep these values beside the environment identity instead of treating them as substitutes for it. A mismatch is a verification failure to resolve, not a reason to change the independently observed environment values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Writing a manifest is not verifying it. Runtime details and dependency pins must come from the actual environment, and a parsed record with a mismatch cannot be declared accurate.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Retrieve the run's commit and dataset generation. Check out and verify the recorded local commit, download and verify the recorded snapshot, and use the pinned Python/dependency environment. Resolve defaults and keyword overrides through the execution function's parameters. Navigate to the recorded directories before resolving relative script or artifact paths, then launch a clean subprocess with captured output and checked exit status. Inspect the captured result rather than assuming launch means completion. In a failure fixture, a changed latest dataset or different working directory should be distinguishable from the recorded execution context. A shell pipe connects one command's output to another's input; it is not the same operation as saving both output streams to a log.

Compare captured resolved parameters with the run record as well as inspecting exit success. A process can exit successfully while using a wrong dataset or default setting, so the reproduction verdict needs identity and configuration checks too. Relative paths are interpreted from the actual working directory; navigate explicitly before invoking the recorded script. The pinned environment and recorded code commit govern which implementation runs, while the verified snapshot governs its inputs. These separate pieces make the bounded reproduction auditable instead of relying on an operator's memory of the previous notebook session.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: The same script filename is not reproduction identity. A changed revision, mutable dataset or unresolved local path can change the executed experiment despite a familiar name.

coverage.learning_objective: Evaluate the frozen selected candidate on protected test observations without retuning.

required_facts.statement: Only evaluate the protected test set after fixing the selected candidate, fitted preprocessing and decision threshold; test results must not choose a replacement candidate or threshold.

required_facts.statement: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.

teaching_blocks.title: Evaluate the Frozen Choice
teaching_blocks.content: The protected test is the final comparison for the already fixed system. Freeze candidate, preprocessing and threshold first; a disappointing test result must be reported rather than used to choose a replacement.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Only evaluate the protected test set after fixing the selected candidate, fitted preprocessing and decision threshold; test results must not choose a replacement candidate or threshold. Generate selected-model and baseline predictions for the same protected-test observations and compare the precommitted predictive quantities on that cohort. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate. With zero cost for correct predictions and supplied deployment class probabilities, expected error cost is P(Y=0) × FPR × cost_FP + P(Y=1) × FNR × cost_FN.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose validation selected candidate B and its threshold, and the protected cohort contains a different observed class mix. Predict that cohort with B and the baseline on the same observations. Use the already fixed deployment probabilities and error costs, not new values chosen to make B pass. Check the precommitted quality and operating requirements and retain the test's actual-class conditioning counts. If B fails the requirement, report failure. A threshold adjustment based on these test outcomes would let the protected observations choose the system, contradicting the boundary. The output is a final matched comparison, not another candidate-selection round.

Freeze means the choices are made before test outcomes are observed: model identity, fitted preprocessing, threshold, metric inputs and requirements all retain their declared values. The baseline and candidate predictions then use the same protected observations for a final matched comparison. Retain the test's observed conditioning counts while applying the supplied deployment probabilities; these are different roles in the calculation. If a required quantity is undefined or a requirement fails, report that outcome explicitly. This protects the interpretation of final testing rather than using it as a source of additional tuning information.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Protected testing is not a second tuning opportunity. Test failure does not authorize switching candidate, refitting preprocessing or searching for a better threshold on those observations.

teaching_blocks.content: An endpoint receives JSON, but a parseable body can still violate the prediction contract. Decode first, then validate fields, types, boundaries and the response alignment before accepting it as a successful prediction request.

teaching_blocks.content: A prediction request schema declares the expected features, their types and permitted values, and a response schema declares the expected output structure. teaching_blocks.content: Send a JSON request body as encoded bytes in urllib.request.Request(url, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST"), then read the response through urlopen with a stated timeout. Use json.dumps to encode structured request/response values and json.loads to decode JSON before checking their fields.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the request contract permits a two-feature matrix with one row per order. A body decoding to three rows of two permitted values can be checked for rank and width, then the response must have the declared row alignment. A body missing a required key fails before prediction. A numeric boundary fixture can test an included limit and a value just beyond it. Send the serialized body as encoded bytes with the declared JSON header and a bounded timeout, decode the returned JSON and inspect its fields. Parsing success, request validity and response correctness are three different checks; retain each failure explicitly rather than returning a successful result for malformed input.

The schema checks must happen before using a field as model input. Check that the required key exists, that its value has the declared type and that its dimensions and values satisfy the stated predicates. A missing key and an out-of-range value are different rejected fixtures. After prediction, inspect the structured response independently: required output keys, row correspondence and declared value or shape expectations. Bounded request timing is part of the fixture transport, not a substitute for contract validation. Explicit rejection distinguishes invalid input from a successful prediction containing the wrong data.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Raw JSON text is not the structured request, and successful JSON decoding is not schema acceptance. A response with the wrong row correspondence still violates the prediction contract.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
In do_POST, read the declared body length from headers and then those bytes from rfile. Decode and validate the request before applying fitted preprocessing and the model, without fit or parameter updates. Encode the named response dictionary as UTF-8 JSON. Write the status and headers, finish the headers and write the body to wfile. Configure the supplied HTTPServer host and port, and exercise the valid, boundary and invalid fixtures. Trace one request through bytes, structured fields, validated model input and encoded output. This keeps request transport and prediction state separate rather than letting every request alter the model.

The byte length describes the encoded response, so compute it from the body actually written rather than from an assumed count of characters. JSON serialization and UTF-8 encoding belong before the response headers that describe that body. On input, Content-Length governs the declared read boundary, while schema checks govern whether decoded content is permitted. Fitted prediction state remains separate from transport handling. The fixture should show a complete bounded request/response exchange with explicit validation, status, headers and body, without turning the standard-library demonstration into a broader production-service design.

teaching_blocks.content: A working http.server fixture is not a production-server recommendation. A response also needs its declared status, content type and body length, not merely a printed prediction.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose five keyed orders are processed in chunks of two, two and one. Apply the fitted preprocessing and model to each chunk, keeping each order key with its prediction. Write that bounded set of serialized results before reading the next chunk. Decode the written fixture again and verify its schema and one-result-per-eligible-key correspondence. A missing key or duplicate output is a failure even if the total number of rows looks reasonable. Keep explicit input and output handles and the declared reader format. The procedure is inference over chunks, not fitting a new model or preprocessor for whichever chunk happens to arrive next.

Keep an output key beside its prediction through serialization, not merely in a temporary input structure. After writing, decode the fixture and compare key coverage against the eligible input IDs. A duplicate result for A plus a missing result for B could leave the total row count unchanged, which is why correspondence needs more than counting rows. Each chunk uses the same fitted objects and declared response schema. The bounded writer and reader handles establish where results were produced and re-inspected. This completes an inference path whose correctness includes persistence and identity, not only in-memory prediction values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A matching total row count does not guarantee one result for every eligible input key. Batch inference preserves keys and fitted state, rather than relying on incidental output order.

teaching_blocks.content: Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Count an attempt as available only for an HTTP 200 response with a valid prediction received within its two-second deadline; allow the final attempt its entire deadline before summarizing. Compute availability as that successful-deadline count divided by 300, including connection-refused and response-timeout attempts that never reach the handler. Reconcile absent handler records with the external failure record and report the probe window, numerator and denominator alongside handler latency/statistics and status counts.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: In the prescribed probe, send one valid request per second in [t0, t0+300 seconds), retaining all 300 attempts. Count success only for HTTP 200 with a valid prediction within two seconds. If 294 qualify, availability is 294/300 = 0.98. Connection refusal and timeouts remain in the denominator even if the handler has no record of them. Allow the final request its whole deadline before summarizing. Instrument JSON decoding, prediction and response encoding, including handled errors, and retain timestamped durations in one unit. Reconcile missing handler records against the external failures instead of computing apparent availability only from requests that arrived.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Handler success rate is not automatically client-visible availability. Excluding attempts that never reached the handler would omit part of the prescribed denominator and conceal failures.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Service telemetry measures prediction delivery independently of model quality; external attempted-request accounting captures unavailability that handler-only metrics cannot observe.

practice_anchor.objective: Instrument one learner-defined prediction handler in the supplied service scaffolding using learner-written imports. practice_anchor.success: The report identifies the probe window, all 300 attempts, and the numerator of HTTP 200 responses containing valid predictions received within two seconds. Availability equals that numerator divided by 300. Connection refusals and response timeouts remain unavailable attempts even without handler records. The report includes an error fraction using the declared external window and denominator, handler status/error counts, latency statistics in a consistent unit, and reconciliation of missing handler records against external outcomes.

At every fixed offered load, use the stated valid payload mix, warm-up and fixed measurement duration, counting successful completions, HTTP errors, timeouts and other failed attempts separately. Compute failed-request fraction from all failed attempts divided by all valid-traffic attempts; timeouts remain failures.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect backlog growth and unfinished work throughout the window; accept only stable-backlog loads meeting the predeclared tail-latency and error limits, and report the highest measured successful throughput or no feasible measured envelope. Use docker run --name NAME -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT --env KEY=VALUE IMAGE to start the referenced image with the declared port and nonsecret runtime settings. Inspect the named container with docker container inspect NAME to check its image identity and State fields.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use docker container logs NAME to inspect its captured standard output and error for initialization or execution failures. Send a JSON request body as encoded bytes in urllib.request.Request(url, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST"), then read the response through urlopen with a stated timeout. Use json.dumps to encode structured request/response values and json.loads to decode JSON before checking their fields.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose 100 valid-traffic attempts in a ten-second window yield 90 successes, six HTTP errors and four timeouts. Success probability is 0.90, failed fraction is 0.10 and successful throughput is 9 per second, while offered load is 10 per second. Compute the declared percentile on completed-latency samples with its convention and units; that sample does not describe timed-out responses. Inspect unfinished work and backlog growth throughout the window. Accept only measured stable-backlog loads meeting fixed latency, error and throughput requirements, or report no feasible envelope. Run intentionally malformed fixtures separately from this valid-traffic measurement so expected rejections do not redefine its denominator.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Arrivals are not completed work. A low latency for completed responses cannot hide timeouts, and a growing backlog is not a stable acceptable load point.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Sustainable serving capacity is successful completed work per unit time under a specified sustained load profile, bounded latency and failure rate; offered request rate alone is not throughput.

practice_anchor.objective: Start and inspect the supplied prediction-service image with its declared published HTTP port and nonsecret settings. Author reusable valid, boundary and malformed JSON fixtures with assertions against the supplied prediction contract. Keep intentional rejection checks separate from capacity measurements. Inspect outcome counts, completed-request latency samples and backlog observations; calculate success probability, failed-request fraction, successful throughput, latency mean, standard deviation and the declared tail percentile. Evaluate each load against predeclared success, throughput, tail-latency and error requirements and backlog stability.
practice_anchor.success: Container identity, State fields and initialization logs are checked, and fixture assertions pass. Each measured load has a report of attempted requests, successful completions, HTTP errors, timeouts, other failures and unfinished work, with the measurement duration and payload profile recorded. Timeouts remain failures in the valid-traffic denominator. The report distinguishes offered rate from successful completions per second, states the completed-latency sample count, time unit and percentile convention, and records backlog behavior throughout the window. It identifies the highest measured successful throughput satisfying all declared requirements with stable backlog, or explicitly reports no feasible measured envelope.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose one request starts at time 1.0, waits until 1.4 for its batch and completes at 1.6. Its end-to-end duration is 0.6 seconds, not the 0.2-second post-wait interval. Decode the successful response and associate it with the request identity and batching setting. Compute the declared tail percentile, mean and specified spread over the eligible successful-response durations in one unit. Compare settings using the same trace and population interpretation, then choose only a limit satisfying the supplied latency objective. Keep the successful-response sample count visible rather than treating a duration list as if it included failures or unmatched responses.

Use a timeline for the same identified request to avoid measuring different intervals under different settings. Start-to-response timing includes the waiting interval, and the selected successful-response population determines which durations enter the percentile. Record the sample count, units and percentile convention so the numerical summary is reproducible. A limit that reduces model-execution time but increases waiting may fail the full latency objective. The supplied trace is evidence about those measured settings and eligible responses; it does not authorize inventing an unmeasured batching configuration or treating unmatched responses as valid duration samples.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Batch waiting belongs in the stated end-to-end latency. A faster execution interval alone does not make a batching limit acceptable under the full request objective.

video_need.reason: A request timeline makes waiting and execution contributions to end-to-end latency visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Decode supplied HTTP JSON request/response traces for two batching limits. Match successful responses to their request identities and settings, compute end-to-end durations including batch waiting, and calculate the mean, standard deviation and declared tail percentile before choosing an eligible limit.
practice_anchor.success: Each duration comes from a matched successful response and equals response completion minus request start in seconds. Both settings use the same population interpretation. Results include successful-response sample counts, mean, standard deviation with the required divisor, and the declared tail percentile with its convention. The selected limit meets the stated latency objective; if neither qualifies, report that neither qualifies.

allowed_syntax: string, integer, floating-point and Boolean literals
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide local JSON request/response traces for two batching settings, using only request identity, batching setting, request-start time, batch-wait end time, response-completion time and success status. Include the illustrative request starting at 1.0 seconds, ending its wait at 1.4 seconds and completing at 1.6 seconds. Supply a latency objective, declared percentile, percentile convention and required standard-deviation divisor. No endpoint calls or runtime changes are required.
live_code.observable_success: Computed result values show correct identity-and-setting matches, exclude unsuccessful or unmatched responses, include waiting in durations, and report reproducible summaries for both settings. A final decision value identifies only a measured setting whose tail latency satisfies the objective, or records that neither setting qualifies.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the identified request's timeline from start at 1.0 seconds through batch-wait end at 1.4 seconds to response completion at 1.6 seconds. Mark the 0.4-second waiting interval, 0.2-second post-wait interval and full 0.6-second end-to-end duration, retaining request identity and batching setting.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Resolve the deployed registry version, artifact source and originating run. Compare that run's dataset, configuration and artifact identities with the deployment and approval record. Download the exact recorded artifact generation and verify its content identity. Inspect the referenced local commit with git rev-parse and git show to confirm that the commit exists, rather than copying a revision string into the audit. In a failure fixture, a deployment linked to artifact B while approval covers A must be flagged. Preserve missing links and mismatches explicitly. The audit connects evidence that exists; it should not infer an unrecorded training source from a familiar model name.

Walk the identity chain in order, comparing deployment to registry, registry to artifact/run, run to recorded configuration and dataset, and code record to the existing commit. Each edge can fail independently, so preserve the missing or mismatched link instead of collapsing every result into a plausible name. The exact-generation download checks content against the lineage record, while local revision inspection checks whether the referenced code exists. context.concept_name: Distinguish data drift, concept drift and observed quality degradation

coverage.learning_objective: Distinguish input shift, changed target relationship and label-supported quality degradation.

required_facts.statement: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality.
Concept drift changes the conditional target relationship P(Y|X), that is, the relationship between features and labels; a previously useful model can become less useful as that relationship changes.
Observed model quality degradation requires comparing predictions with corresponding ground-truth labels and the declared quality reference.
Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality. teaching_blocks.content: Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a production window contains more long-distance orders than the reference. That is evidence about P(X), the input distribution. It does not establish that P(Y|X), the target relationship conditional on features, changed. To claim observed quality degradation, compare predictions with their corresponding ground truth and the declared quality reference. If matched available labels are absent, record the supported distribution or service observation and the unresolved quality question. Conversely, a conditional target relationship can change in the concept-drift sense even when an input summary is not the evidence that reveals it. Keep the three questions distinct rather than calling every change ‘the model got worse.’

Separate an operational report into what is observed and what is unresolved. More long-distance inputs support an input-distribution statement. Matched labels compared with the quality reference support an observed-error statement. Conditional-target evidence addresses whether the feature/label relationship changed. The absence of labels does not prove that quality stayed constant; it means the labeled-quality question is not yet measured by that evidence. Likewise, input drift does not prove that quality worsened. Keeping these distinctions preserves uncertainty without discarding useful distribution or service evidence, and prevents a response justified by one type of evidence from being mislabeled as another.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare active artifact/configuration identities with the approved deployment and run. If a schema fixture fails, investigate that data condition; if a distribution differs, do not equate it with measured labeled degradation. Calculate release/cohort error rates only on matched eligible mature labels, retaining distinct denominators. Reproduce and isolate the regression from the timeline and test one causal hypothesis. Choose only the policy-supported action justified by evidence: supplied data repair, approved rollback or gated retraining. Preserve required validation. A different class mix or incomplete labels cannot be silently treated as a causal model regression simply because they appeared after deployment.

Test the selected hypothesis against evidence that can distinguish it from alternatives. An artifact mismatch supports a different investigation from a schema defect, and neither is established merely by a distribution difference. Matched mature-label rates need their own release/cohort counts, so incomplete labels are not treated as successful predictions. Keep the incident response within the existing policy and its authorization boundary. After choosing the supported data repair, rollback or retraining path, preserve the corresponding validation gates and audit evidence. The diagnosis is bounded to the reproduced regression and available evidence rather than a blanket explanation of all model errors.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose an investigated distribution signal satisfies the existing entry policy for an authorized identity. Record it as distribution evidence rather than labeled error, and bind the intended dataset. Annotate existing quality/test, training and evaluation stages with their artifact inputs and purposes. Trace the eligible event through required dependencies, then trace a failed data check to show where downstream execution stops. Test entry rejection for an unauthorized identity or an uninvestigated alarm. Keep later promotion dependent on its own approval. Handoff credentials remain runtime-injected and absent from policy values, YAML and captured logs.

A schedule event and a verified performance event may both be allowed trigger types, but their recorded reasons should retain the actual evidence used. Distribution-only evidence remains distribution-only even if it permits retraining under policy. Trace dataset identity across entry and quality checks so a permitted event cannot silently train on an unintended input. A failed required check blocks its downstream path; a completed retraining path still leaves promotion approval separate. The operational record should bind trigger reason, authorized identity, intended artifacts and dependency outcomes without exposing runtime credential values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Retraining eligibility is not deployment approval. A distribution-only signal must not be relabeled as measured prediction degradation, and an alarm is not automatically an authorized trigger.

Distinguish label-verified quality evidence from distribution-only evidence. Annotate the data-quality/test, training, evaluation and separately authorized promotion stages with their purposes and required input artifacts. Trace one eligible event and one failed check, and reject an unauthorized identity or uninvestigated alarm at entry. Keep credentials runtime-injected rather than embedded in policy values or handoff records.
practice_anchor.success: The completed policy justifies each eligibility decision from supplied evidence and preserves the intended dataset at handoff. The eligible-event trace follows the existing entry stage and every required dependency without bypassing tests or evaluation. The failed-check trace identifies precisely which dependent downstream stages cannot execute. Unauthorized identities and uninvestigated alarms are rejected at entry. Completing retraining does not authorize promotion: promotion retains its own approval requirement. Credential values are absent from the policy, YAML values and captured stage logs. No new pipeline is implemented, no execution is invoked and no candidate is automatically promoted.

coverage.learning_objective: Use the supplied durable admission and executor contracts to prevent duplicate or overlapping logical runs.

required_facts.statement: Read the declared run key and pipeline identity from the dictionary event record, and pass them to the supplied durable coordinator’s atomic admission operation.

Handle returned accepted, duplicate and busy statuses with explicit conditional branches: only an accepted reservation authorizes a new logical launch.

teaching_blocks.content: Pass run key K and pipeline identity to the single atomic admission operation. If accepted, use its persisted job ID J as the executor's idempotency token. A duplicate or restarted claim resumes or attaches to J; an unknown launch result is reconciled with that same token rather than replaced by J2. A different key facing the active slot follows the busy defer/reject policy without launching. Release the slot only after confirmed terminal state while retaining K's completed record. Test concurrent same-key workers, different-key contention and fresh workers after both reservation and launch, asserting durable state and logical job count. Keep required pipeline gates fatal.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A process-local dictionary or separate check-then-write calls cannot supply the durable atomic admission contract. A retry must not invent a new job identity, and releasing an active slot before terminal confirmation permits the wrong overlap.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Durable atomic admission owns the run key and active slot; a stable persisted job identity closes the reservation-to-launch crash gap. Local checks and sequential replay alone cannot establish distributed idempotency.

practice_anchor.success: Concurrent same-event workers produce one logical job; different keys cannot hold overlapping active jobs for the same pipeline. Fresh workers after reservation, launch or an unknown launch response reconcile using the same persisted job ID. Terminal confirmation permits slot release while the retained completed key prevents relaunch. Tests assert durable state and logical job count. The reloaded configuration has the required execution image, entry point and dependency IDs, and actual accepted and rejected trigger fixtures demonstrate the configured input bindings and fatal gate behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the candidate has lower expected cost than the incumbent but fails a required slice check. Reject it under the fixed gate policy. Calculate both costs with the same supplied deployment probabilities, error costs and actual-class conditional rates. A missing conditioning group does not provide a defined rate. Keep protected-test observations out of fitting and setting choice. Bind the exact registry/artifact identity and verdict to the controlled promotion record, with assertion fixtures for accepted, boundary and failed cases. Approval evidence for candidate A must not be reused for candidate B just because both came from the same retraining pipeline.

The incumbent and candidate must be evaluated under the same fixed validation question before their expected costs are comparable. Keep quality, required slices and deployment compatibility as separately named gate results. A cost improvement does not erase a compatibility failure, and a complete gate record for one identity cannot be transferred to another. Accepted, boundary and rejected fixtures should verify both verdict and identity binding. Promotion evidence therefore states which exact candidate passed which requirements, rather than merely saying that the latest retraining run produced a model with a better number.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Retrained does not mean accepted. An aggregate gain cannot bypass a required slice or compatibility gate, and validation of one artifact does not approve another.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect instance identity, state and process/service evidence and retain the fault record. Under the approved identity, stop the same authorized instance, wait, start it and wait until running. Reconnect and inspect the restored model service. Verify readiness and a bounded prediction exchange against the expected contract rather than assuming a running VM means recovery. Keep credentials in the existing runtime mechanism and out of commands, configuration and captured output. Record state before and after the action. This is a runbook-scoped nonproduction fixture, not permission to restart unrelated resources or broaden the recovery policy.

The pre-recovery evidence is important because stop/start can change process state and remove the immediate fault symptom. Inspect the authorized instance before acting, record what failed and test the runbook's supported hypothesis. After start completes, reconnect and compare model-service state and endpoint behavior with the expected contract. A running instance state is a lifecycle observation; readiness and a successful bounded prediction are service observations. Retain both in the same recovery record along with authorized target identity. This verifies the supplied recovery procedure without assuming that a restart of an arbitrary resource would be safe or sufficient.

teaching_blocks.content: Restarting a VM is not proof that model service behavior recovered. The authorized target, fault evidence and post-restart readiness/prediction checks all belong in the recovery verdict.

Resource samples need both units and identity. CPU percent and memory units are not interchangeable columns, and their descriptive summaries should cover the same matched workload interval. The lifecycle record helps distinguish a stopped instance from an active measurement window. Process inspection adds evidence that the workload named in the report was actually running. These summaries characterize resource usage during the bounded task; they do not independently establish billed cost, request success or model quality.

clusters.title: Training-Fitted Feature Transformations
clusters.reasoning: Imputation, numerical scaling and categorical encoding are adjacent variants of the same fit-on-training, reuse-on-validation operation. Each retains its own replacement, scaling or category policy rather than becoming an interchangeable transformation. All prerequisites are available before this tile. Pipeline composition remains a separate later concept because it requires these fitted transformations.

clusters.title: Validation-Based Selection Under Task Costs
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent steps apply precommitted validation cost and eligibility rules to freeze a prediction choice before protected testing. Keep their selection objects explicit: threshold selection changes the cutoff for scores, whereas candidate comparison ranks supplied model records against a baseline. Metrics, acceptance criteria and their prerequisites are available at tile start; neither concept requires the other as preparation.

clusters.title: Localize Errors Across Validation Groups
clusters.reasoning: Both concepts examine conditional errors within an identified validation group rather than treating the overall score as sufficient. Error analysis investigates recurring failures; slice evaluation compares predefined groups with their counts and representativeness limits. These are complementary views of one diagnostic workflow, with metric prerequisites already available at tile start. Subgroup mitigation stays separate because it requires slice evaluation.

clusters.title: Record and Control Training Comparisons
clusters.reasoning: Run logging and random-source control are adjacent parts of a traceable training comparison: record configuration, metrics and artifacts, then make the random settings and observed variability explicit. A recorded run is not itself a guarantee of deterministic reproduction, and seed control does not provide that guarantee either. Both prerequisite sets precede the tile. Regularization remains its own model-selection step; search remains separate and requires the randomness concept.

clusters.title: Training Updates and Forward-Only Validation
clusters.reasoning: The minibatch update loop and training/evaluation mode handling are parts of one neural training workflow. The shared explanation must keep parameter-updating training distinct from forward-only validation, including the separate roles of eval mode and disabled gradient recording. Both concepts have all prerequisites before tile start. Weight persistence remains separate because it requires training/evaluation modes.

clusters.title: Measure Training Bottlenecks and Capacity
clusters.reasoning: Profiling a bounded workload and comparing authorized CPU/GPU capacity are adjacent evidence-gathering parts of choosing a suitable training runtime. Keep operator/data-loading attribution distinct from the matched runtime, memory and billing comparison; profiling is not a prerequisite for the supplied hardware comparison. All declared prerequisites precede this tile, so neither sub-concept needs knowledge introduced by its neighbor.

clusters.title: Capture Dataset and Environment Identity
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts capture complementary immutable inputs to a reproducible training record: the selected dataset generation/hash and the actual code revision, dependency pins and runtime identity. They are parts of one provenance-capture operation, not claims that an environment manifest versions the dataset. Both prerequisite sets are available at tile start. Script conversion stays separate; experiment reproduction follows only after these records and the script exist.

clusters.title: Prepare a Traceable Model Release Artifact
clusters.reasoning: Registration and packaging are adjacent parts of preparing an identifiable model deliverable. Registration links the immutable artifact to its originating run; packaging carries fitted preprocessing, model state and compatible inference dependencies and checks reloaded predictions. Keep those distinct responsibilities explicit rather than treating registration as proof of package correctness. Every prerequisite for both concepts precedes the tile.

clusters.title: Reproduce and Verify a Model Deployment
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts form a deployment workflow around an immutable artifact and explicit runtime configuration: reproduce the deployment, then inspect its identity and prediction behavior. Configuration validity and successful startup are not substitutes for release verification. Both prerequisite sets are already available at tile start, so the supplied verification task does not depend on first learning its neighboring configuration concept.

clusters.title: Measure and Tune Bounded Serving Capacity
clusters.reasoning: Load testing, batching selection and bounded worker concurrency are adjacent parts of checking serving performance under fixed service constraints. Keep endpoint-level throughput and tail latency, request batching limits and actual worker bounds distinct; batching and concurrency are not interchangeable controls. All prerequisites precede the tile. Replica scaling stays separate because it requires the load-test concept introduced here.

clusters.title: Fail-Closed Data, Behavior and Release Gates
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are variants of the same operation: evaluate named requirements, retain failure evidence and stop dependent pipeline or promotion steps on rejection. Preserve separate scopes and evidence: dataset validity before training, packaged inference behavior on fixtures, and candidate acceptance before release. Passing one is not passing the others. All prerequisite sets are available at the beginning of this tile.
